claim: Influenza virus penetrates cells by fusion of viral and endosomal membranes catalyzed by the viral hemagglutinin (HA).
source: Influenza virus penetrates cells by fusion of viral and endosomal membranes catalyzed by the viral hemagglutinin (HA).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the manuscript's introduction and background context.

claim: Fusion requires engagement of three or four neighboring HA trimers.
source: fusion then requires engagement of three or four neighboring HA trimers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from single-virion fusion kinetics and gamma distribution analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Withdrawal of the fusion peptide from a pocket in the pre-fusion trimer is rate-limiting for both arrest and hemifusion events.
source: Effects of mutations in HA indicate that withdrawal of the fusion peptide from a pocket in the pre-fusion trimer is rate-limiting for both events
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from site-directed mutagenesis experiments showing that mutations affecting fusion peptide stability alter fusion kinetics.

claim: A long-lived intermediate state exists for single, extended HA trimers.
source: the requirement for cooperative action of several HAs to bring the fusing membranes together leads to a long-lived intermediate state for single, extended HA trimers.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data showing different rates for arrest and hemifusion, and supported by computer simulation.

claim: HA is a homotrimer synthesized as an inactive precursor [HA0]3 and activated for fusion by proteolytic cleavage into HA1 and HA2.
source: HA is a homotrimer, synthesized as an inactive precursor, [HA0]3, and activated for fusion by proteolytic cleavage of each chain into HA1 and HA2, yielding [HA1-HA2]3.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HA structure and activation, referenced in the introduction.

claim: At the N-terminus of HA2 is a hydrophobic 'fusion peptide' which inserts into a pocket near the axis of the trimer following cleavage.
source: At the N-terminus of HA2 is a hydrophobic 'fusion peptide', which following cleavage inserts firmly into a pocket near the axis of the trimer (Chen et al., 1998).
evidence: This structural feature is supported by citation to Chen et al., 1998.

claim: Exposure to low pH causes the HA1 'head' to separate from the HA2 'stem' and enables HA2 conformational transformations.
source: Exposure to low pH, which during infection occurs in an endosome, causes the HA1 'head' to separate from the HA2 'stem' and enables a set of HA2 conformational transformations
evidence: This is established knowledge about HA mechanism, supported by structural studies.

claim: HA2 conformational transformations include: (1) release of the fusion peptide from its pre-fusion pocket; (2) HA2 extension; (3) insertion of the fusion peptide into the target membrane; (4) fold-back of the extended HA2 intermediate.
source: (1) release of the fusion peptide from its pre-fusion pocket; (2) HA2 extension; (3) insertion of the fusion peptide into the target membrane; (4) fold-back of the extended HA2 intermediate (Figure 1A) (Skehel and Wiley, 2000).
evidence: This sequence of events is supported by citation to Skehel and Wiley, 2000, and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Floyd et al. (2008) devised a method to monitor in real time the fusion of individual influenza virus particles with planar bilayers.
source: Floyd et al. (2008) devised a method to monitor in real time the fusion of individual influenza virus particles with planar bilayers.
evidence: This is a citation to previous work that established the experimental method.

claim: Floyd et al. (2008) concluded that fusion requires on average three HA trimers, each of which independently undergoes the same, rate-limiting rearrangement.
source: Their results led to the conclusion that fusion requires on average three HA trimers, each of which independently undergoes the same, rate-limiting rearrangement
evidence: This is a citation to the conclusions of Floyd et al. (2008).

claim: Upon initiating the flow of buffer for pH exchange, most virions started to move under the hydrodynamic force while retaining contacts with the target bilayer.
source: Upon initiating the flow of buffer for pH exchange, most virions started to move under the hydrodynamic force while retaining contacts with the target bilayer.
evidence: This observation is directly reported from the experimental data.

claim: Virion arrest was irreversible and invariably preceded hemifusion.
source: The particles arrested at various times after the pH drop, but invariably preceding hemifusion (Figure 1B; Video 1). The arrest was irreversible (Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in videos and figures.

claim: Approximately 20% of virions at pH 5.5 and 5.65 had already arrested at the onset of imaging or had done so before the pH drop.
source: A subset (approximately 20% at pH 5.5 and 5.65) of virions had already arrested at the onset of imaging or had done so before the pH drop.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experimental data.

claim: For lower final pH, a larger fraction of virions had arrested by the time the pH drop was complete.
source: For lower final pH, a larger fraction had arrested by the time the pH drop was complete (Table 1).
evidence: This observation is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: Mean values for tlag(pHdrop–arrest) and tlag(arrest–hemifusion) show the same pH dependence, with mean tlag(pHdrop–arrest) being about an order of magnitude shorter throughout the tested pH range.
source: Mean values for tlag(pHdrop–arrest) and tlag(arrest–hemifusion) show the same pH dependence, with mean tlag(pHdrop–arrest) being about an order of magnitude shorter throughout the tested pH range.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of experimental measurements across pH conditions.

claim: The distributions for both tlag(pHdrop–arrest) and tlag(arrest–hemifusion) can be fit with a gamma distribution describing a requirement for N independent events.
source: We can fit the distributions for both tlag(pHdrop–arrest) and tlag(arrest–hemifusion) with one describing a requirement for N independent events (either parallel or sequential; Feller, 1968), each with rate constant, k (Figure 1C and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data, with citation to the mathematical framework.

claim: For any given particle, the two lag times (arrest and hemifusion) are uncorrelated, ruling out any mutual dependence on overall particle properties such as length.
source: For any given particle, the two lag times are uncorrelated, ruling out any mutual dependence on overall particle properties such as length (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an inference from the data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: N = 3–4 both for the number of events required to arrest virions following pH drop and for the number of events required for hemifusion of the arrested particle.
source: From the distributions, we derive N = 3–4 both for the number of events required to arrest virions following pH drop (Figure 1E and Table 1) and for the number of events required for hemifusion of the arrested particle (Figure 1F and Table 1)
evidence: This is derived from gamma distribution fitting of experimental data.

claim: Insertion of fusion peptides from 3 or 4 independent HA trimers into the target membrane anchors the particle.
source: A simple interpretation of virion arrest is that insertion of fusion peptides from a number of independent HA trimers (3 or 4) into the target membrane anchors the particle.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations based on the kinetic data.

claim: Bulk experiments have shown that short incubations of virions with target membranes at pH 5 and 0°C lead to insertion of a small subset of fusion peptides and stable virus anchoring not associated with membrane fusion.
source: Bulk experiments have shown that short incubations of virions with target membranes at pH 5 and 0°C lead to insertion of a small subset of fusion peptides and stable virus anchoring not associated with membrane fusion (Tsurudome et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsurudome et al., 1992.

claim: Recombinant virions with Udorn HA had shorter hemifusion lag times in the physiologically relevant pH regime (pH > 4.5) than those with X-31 HA.
source: Nonetheless, recombinant virions with Udorn HA had shorter hemifusion lag times in the physiologically relevant pH regime (pH > 4.5) than did those with X-31 HA (Figure 3A, Videos 1 and 4).
evidence: This is a direct comparison of experimental measurements between two HA variants.

claim: Udorn-HA particles did not show directed motion under flow at any observable time point—they had arrested by the time the low-pH transition was complete.
source: Moreover, the Udorn-HA particles did not show directed motion under flow at any observable time point—that is, they had arrested by the time the low-pH transition was complete
evidence: This is an experimental observation comparing Udorn and X-31 HA behavior.

claim: The Udorn hemifusion lag time distribution between pH 5.65 and 4 gave a pH-independent value of N close to 3.
source: The Udorn hemifusion lag time (tlag(pHdrop–hemifusion)) distribution between pH 5.65 and 4 gave a pH-independent value of N close to 3 (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is derived from gamma distribution fitting of experimental data for Udorn HA.

claim: Differences between Udorn and X31 HAs do not affect the number of rate-limiting steps between virion arrest and hemifusion, but only their individual rate constants.
source: showing that differences between Udorn and X31 HAs do not affect the number of rate-limiting steps between virion arrest and hemifusion, but only their individual rate constants (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the kinetic parameters of the two HA variants.

claim: Udorn is the only strain in the database with a serine substitution at position four in HA2, with glycine being otherwise universally conserved.
source: Udorn is the only strain in the database with this substitution, glycine being otherwise universally conserved (Nobusawa et al., 1991; Cross et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to database analyses.

claim: In the pre-fusion conformation of HA, Gly4HA2 participates in a network of polar hydrogen-bond interactions with the carboxylate of Asp112 HA2, which is also strictly conserved.
source: In the pre-fusion conformation of HA, Gly4HA2 participates in a network of polar hydrogen-bond interactions with the carboxylate of Asp112 HA2, which is also strictly conserved (Figure 3D) (Wilson et al., 1981; Weis et al., 1990; Russell et al., 2004).
evidence: This structural information is supported by multiple citations to crystallographic studies.

claim: A serine substitution at Gly4HA2 would weaken or interrupt the interaction with Asp112HA2, because glycine has a backbone conformation not allowed for other residues.
source: A serine substitution would weaken or interrupt this interaction, because the glycine has a backbone conformation not allowed for other residues.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural chemistry knowledge.

claim: Previous studies have reported an elevated pH threshold of fusion for cell-surface expressed HA harboring substitutions at Gly4 or Asp112.
source: Previous studies have reported an elevated pH threshold of fusion for cell-surface expressed HA harboring substitutions at Gly4 or Asp112 (Gething et al., 1986; Steinhauer et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: The mutation G4SHA2X31 accelerates hemifusion, and the reverse mutation S4GHA2Udorn retards it.
source: The mutation G4SHA2X31 indeed accelerates hemifusion, and the reverse mutation S4GHA2Udorn retards it (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from site-directed mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Like WT Udorn virions, G4SHA2X31 virions do not show flow-induced motion at pH drop, while 76% S4GHA2Udorn virions do.
source: Moreover, like WT Udorn virions, G4SHA2X31 virions do not show flow-induced motion at pH drop, while 76% S4GHA2Udorn virions do (Videos 5 and 6, Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental observation comparing mutant behaviors.

claim: Kinetic parameters for arrest derived from the tlag(pHdrop–arrest) distribution for S4GHA2Udorn particles are indistinguishable from those for X31-HA WT.
source: Kinetic parameters for arrest, derived from the tlag(pHdrop–arrest) distribution for the S4GHA2Udorn particles are indistinguishable from those for X31-HA WT (Figure 4C and Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of kinetic parameters from experimental data.

claim: A single mutation (G4S/S4G), and thus probably the same molecular process, affects both the rate of arrest and the rate of hemifusion.
source: These observations show that a single mutation, and thus probably the same molecular process, affects both the rate of arrest and the rate of hemifusion.
evidence: This is an inference from the mutational analysis data.

claim: D112AHA2 mutations accelerate hemifusion of both Udorn and X31-HA virions, but the effect on the latter is more pronounced.
source: D112AHA2 mutations accelerate hemifusion of both Udorn and X31-HA virions, but the effect on the latter is more pronounced (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from site-directed mutagenesis experiments.

claim: The G4SHA2 mutation partly destabilizes contacts between the terminal fusion-peptide residues and Asp112HA2, and the D112AHA2 change eliminates this source of stability completely.
source: We infer from these observations that the G4SHA2 mutation partly destabilizes contacts between the terminal fusion-peptide residues and Asp112HA2 and that the D112AHA2 change then eliminates this source of stability completely.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparative mutational analysis.

claim: None of the mutations change the values of N derived from the pH 5.5 tlag(arrest–hemifusion) distributions.
source: None of the mutations change the values of N derived from the pH 5.5 tlag(arrest–hemifusion) distributions (or for static virions, tlag(pHdrop–hemifusion) distributions) (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from gamma distribution analysis of mutant data.

claim: For these viruses, release of the fusion peptide from its pre-fusion pocket is a rate-limiting step in the transition from arrest to hemifusion.
source: We conclude that for these viruses, release of the fusion peptide from its pre-fusion pocket is a rate-limiting step in the transition from arrest to hemifusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis showing that mutations affecting fusion peptide stability alter kinetics.

claim: N is related to the number of HA trimers that must independently expose their fusion peptides before a hemifusion-inducing transition can follow.
source: further support our proposal that N is related to the number of HA trimers that must independently expose their fusion peptides before a hemifusion-inducing transition can follow.
evidence: This is an inference from the consistent changes in fusion kinetics produced by mutations and the gamma distribution analysis.

claim: At pH 4.5 and below, the mutants have indistinguishable mean values for tlag(pHdrop–hemifusion).
source: At pH 4.5 and below, the mutants described above have indistinguishable mean values for tlag(pHdrop–hemifusion) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from experimental measurements at low pH.

claim: The lag times have become nearly pH independent at pH 4.5 and below, presumably because most of the relevant titrating groups (carboxylates) have become protonated.
source: Moreover, the lag times have become nearly pH independent, presumably because most of the relevant titrating groups (carboxylates) have become protonated.
evidence: This is an inference based on chemical knowledge about protonation states at different pH values.

claim: Fitting the tlag(pHdrop–hemifusion) distributions at pH 4.5 with a gamma probability density yields unchanged values of N (between 3 and 6) for all the variants.
source: Fitting the tlag(pHdrop–hemifusion) distributions with a gamma probability density yields unchanged values of N (between 3 and 6) for all the variants, confirming that what changes with pH is not the number of rate-limiting rearrangements leading to hemifusion but only their rate (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is derived from statistical analysis of experimental data at pH 4.5.

claim: Protonation of Asp112 probably explains why mutations that affect stability of the fusion peptide in its pre-fusion pocket and influence the fusion rate at pH 5.5 have little or no effect on the fusion rate at pH 4.5 and below.
source: Protonation of Asp112 probably explains why mutations that affect stability of the fusion peptide in its pre-fusion pocket and influence the fusion rate at pH 5.5 have little or no effect on the fusion rate at pH 4.5 and below.
evidence: This is an inference based on chemical knowledge about protonation and the mutational data.

claim: The steps determining the rate of arrest and the rate of transition from arrest to hemifusion are the same—both processes are limited by the rate of fusion-peptide exposure.
source: The influence of mutations at positions 4 and 112 in HA2 on hemifusion at the physiologically relevant pH of 5.5 demonstrates that the steps determining the rate of arrest (from the time of pH drop) and the rate of transition from arrest to hemifusion are the same, that is, both processes are limited by the rate of fusion-peptide exposure.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis showing similar effects on both processes.

claim: Both arrest and hemifusion result from the action of several HA trimers each undergoing the rate-limiting rearrangement independently, as indicated by the unchanged shape of their individual lag time distributions under vastly different proton concentrations.
source: Both also result from the action of several HA trimers each undergoing this rate-limiting rearrangement as indicated by the unchanged shape of their individual lag time distributions (unchanged value of N) under vastly different proton concentrations (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference from the gamma distribution analysis across different pH conditions.

claim: The rate constants derived from gamma distribution fitting of the tlag(pHdrop–arrest) data are about five to tenfold greater than those for tlag(arrest-hemifusion).
source: The rate constants derived from gamma distribution fitting of the tlag(pHdrop–arrest) data are, however, about five to tenfold greater than those for tlag(arrest-hemifusion) (Figure 1)
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of rate constants derived from experimental data analysis.

claim: Virion arrest results from fusion-peptide release and irreversible target-membrane insertion from several HA trimers anywhere in the area of virus-target membrane contact.
source: A simple interpretation of these observations is that virion arrest results from fusion-peptide release and irreversible target-membrane insertion from several HA trimers anywhere in the area of virus-target membrane contact
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations based on the kinetic data and mutational analysis.

claim: Hemifusion is limited by fusion-peptide release and membrane insertion but requires a specific geometry for the participating HAs—their proximity to each other.
source: hemifusion is limited by the same HA rearrangements, fusion-peptide release and membrane insertion, but requires a specific geometry for the participating HAs, that is, their proximity to each other, and is thus related to a different probability.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations explaining the different rate constants for arrest and hemifusion.

claim: The lower-limit estimate of a contact area can accommodate up to about 50 HA trimers, based on dimensions of a spherical virion with 55 nm in membrane-to-membrane diameter.
source: Our lower-limit estimate of a contact area that can accommodate up to about 50 HA trimers, shown in Figure 6, is based on dimensions of a spherical virion with 55 nm in membrane-to-membrane diameter (Calder et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a calculation based on cited structural data.

claim: Virions used in the experiments are on average approximately 130 nm long and 55 nm wide, and the actual contact area can on average accommodate up to about 120 HA trimers.
source: Virions used in our current experiments are on average approximately 130 nm long and 55 nm wide (Ivanovic et al., 2012; see 'Materials and methods'), and thus the actual contact area can on average accommodate up to about 120 HA trimers.
evidence: This is based on measurements of virion dimensions and geometric calculations.

claim: Simulation-derived distributions agree remarkably well with experimentally obtained data and predict Na = 3–4, Nh = 3–4 and are most consistent with a contact patch area of approximately 120 HAs.
source: Simulation-derived distributions agree remarkably well with our experimentally obtained data and predict Na = 3–4, Nh = 3–4 and are most consistent with our independently predicted contact patch area of approximately 120 HAs (Figure 5B, i and ii).
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing computer simulation results with experimental data.

claim: The gamma-distribution-derived value of N for virion arrest closely approximates the number of trimers leading to arrest, Na.
source: The gamma-distribution-derived value of N for virion arrest closely approximates the number of trimers leading to arrest, Na, but the apparent rate constant is substantially higher than the rate constant governing HA extension and membrane insertion (Figure 5A, i).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the computer simulation analysis.

claim: The gamma-distribution-derived value of N for hemifusion is related to the number of neighboring HA trimers participating in hemifusion, but it only approximates this value for smaller contact patch sizes and is greater than the true Nh for larger patch sizes.
source: The gamma-distribution-derived value of N for hemifusion is related to the number of neighboring HA trimers participating in hemifusion, but it only approximates this value for smaller contact patch sizes (close to 50 HA trimers) and is greater than the true Nh for larger patch sizes (Figure 5B, i).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the computer simulation analysis showing the relationship between apparent and true N values.

claim: The value of Nh = 2 yields a distribution that cannot be approximated by a gamma distribution for any analyzed patch size and value of Na.
source: The value of Nh = 2 yields a distribution that cannot be approximated by a gamma distribution for any analyzed patch size and value of Na (see Figure 5A, ii, for one such example).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the computer simulation analysis.

claim: The value of Nh = 5 yields a gamma distribution value of N > 5 for all analyzed patch sizes and N close to 7 for the predicted patch size of approximately 120 HA trimers, inconsistent with experimentally derived values.
source: Likewise, the value of Nh = 5 yields a gamma distribution value of N > 5 for all analyzed patch sizes and N close to 7 for the predicted patch size of approximately 120 HA trimers (Figure 5B, i), inconsistent with our experimentally derived values.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing simulation results with experimental data.

claim: The experimental data are consistent with Nh = 3–4 for patch sizes between 50 and 150 HA trimers.
source: Our experimental data—the gamma-distribution-derived N and the ratio of mean hemifusion and arrest times—are consistent with Nh = 3–4 for patch sizes between 50 and 150 HA trimers.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing simulation predictions with experimental observations.

claim: The apparent N-value-range between 3 and 6 corresponds to the actual Nh range between 3 and 4 and a patch size of about 120.
source: The apparent N-value-range between 3 and 6 (as observed for various mutants in Figure 4) corresponds to the actual Nh range between 3 and 4 and a patch size of about 120.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation analysis relating apparent and true parameter values.

claim: The key parameters (gamma-distribution-derived N value and the ratio of mean hemifusion and arrest lag times) are independent of the percentage of active HAs within the contact patch, down to a lattice-point occupancy of 40%.
source: We found that the key parameters—the gamma-distribution-derived N value and the ratio of mean hemifusion and arrest lag times—are independent of the percentage of active HAs within the contact patch, down to a lattice-point occupancy of 40% (Figure 5B, iii).
evidence: This is a conclusion from simulation analysis testing robustness to irregularities.

claim: Reduction in active HA density to 20% yielded a sudden drop in the apparent N derived from gamma-distribution fitting of simulation-derived tlag(arrest–hemifusion) data, consistent with previously published experimental evidence at pH 3.
source: Further reduction in active HA density to 20% yielded a sudden drop in the apparent N derived from gamma-distribution fitting of simulation-derived tlag(arrest–hemifusion) data, consistent with previously published experimental evidence at pH 3, a proton concentration suggested to induce substantial HA denaturation (Floyd et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a comparison of simulation results with previously published experimental data.

claim: Early studies of HA-mediated fusion kinetics relied on fusion of HA-expressing cells with red blood cells or planar bilayers.
source: Many early studies of HA-mediated fusion kinetics relied on fusion of HA-expressing cells with red blood cells (Spruce et al., 1989; Zimmerberg et al., 1994) or planar bilayers (Melikyan et al., 1993a, 1993b).
evidence: This is a summary of previous work supported by citations.

claim: Measurements of conductance and capacitance in planar bilayer experiments showed reversible opening and closing of flickering pores, following initial acidification and commitment to secure pore opening only after a number of seconds.
source: In the latter case, measurements of conductance and capacitance showed reversible opening and closing of flickering pores, following initial acidification and commitment to secure pore opening only after a number of seconds.
evidence: This is a summary of previous experimental observations.

claim: Single-virion fusion experiments confirmed the earlier estimate of 3–4 HAs and showed that lipid-mixing precedes content mixing, as expected for an obligatory hemifusion intermediate.
source: Single-virion fusion experiments confirmed the earlier estimate of 3–4 HAs and showed that lipid-mixing precedes content mixing, as expected for an obligatory hemifusion intermediate (Floyd et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a citation to previous single-virion experiments.

claim: In Floyd et al. (2008), the single, rate-limiting step for content mixing had a rate constant of about 0.05/s.
source: In that work, the single, rate-limiting step for content mixing had a rate constant of about 0.05/s.
evidence: This is a citation to a specific quantitative result from previous work.

claim: The pathway with the lowest energy barrier for hemifusion appears to be through a 'hemifusion stalk', derived from the apposed leaflets.
source: The pathway with the lowest energy barrier appears to be through a so-called 'hemifusion stalk', derived from the apposed leaflets (Kuzmin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on calculations and cited work on membrane fusion mechanisms.

claim: Some proposals for the transition from stalk to fusion pore postulate expansion of the stalk into a 'hemifusion diaphragm'; others suggest that a stalk can open directly into a pore.
source: Some proposals for the subsequent transition to a fusion pore postulate expansion of the stalk into a 'hemifusion diaphragm', in which the distal leaflets form a continuous bilayer between the two membrane-bounded compartments; others suggest that a stalk can open directly into a pore.
evidence: This is a summary of different theoretical proposals in the field.

claim: Hemifusion diaphragms can be seen by electron microscopy.
source: Hemifusion diaphragms can be seen by electron microscopy (e.g., Hernandez et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to electron microscopy studies.

claim: Evidence for stalk-like structures comes from x-ray analysis of crystalline lipid phases.
source: evidence for stalk-like structures comes from x-ray analysis of crystalline lipid phases (Yang and Huang, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to x-ray crystallography studies.

claim: Both calculations and observations suggest that hemifusion diaphragms are stable, long-lived intermediates and that their formation might be a dead-end side reaction.
source: Both calculations and observations suggest that hemifusion diaphragms are stable, long-lived intermediates and that their formation might be a dead-end side reaction.
evidence: This is a summary of conclusions from theoretical and experimental work in the field.

claim: Recent work on calcium-triggered SNARE/synaptotagmin/complexin-mediated fusion shows that the reaction proceeds too quickly (<100 ms) to detect even a hemifusion intermediate and that fusion from a hemifusion diaphragm is slow (tens of seconds) and inefficient.
source: Recent work on calcium-triggered SNARE/synaptotagmin/complexin-mediated fusion of lipid vesicles on a physiological time scale shows that the reaction proceeds too quickly (<100 ms) to detect even a hemifusion intermediate and that fusion from a hemifusion diaphragm is slow (tens of seconds) and inefficient (Diao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a citation to recent work on SNARE-mediated fusion.

claim: In influenza-virus fusion, tight packing of proteins on the viral surface probably makes a transition from stalk or other point-contact intermediate to diaphragm even less likely than in SNARE-mediated fusion.
source: In influenza-virus fusion, tight packing of proteins on the viral surface probably makes a transition from stalk or other point-contact intermediate to diaphragm even less likely than in SNARE-mediated fusion, in which protein coverage of the fusing membranes is sparser.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing protein density in different fusion systems.

claim: The experiments provide strong evidence for a long-lived, extended HA intermediate and for a rapid and cooperative transition to lipid mixing when a critical number of these intermediates has accumulated within a contact neighborhood.
source: They provide strong evidence for a long-lived, extended HA intermediate and for a rapid and cooperative transition to lipid mixing when a critical number of these intermediates has accumulated within a contact neighborhood.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: HA trimers independently undergo the first part of their low-pH-induced conformational change and pause as extended intermediates with their fusion peptides inserted into the target membrane.
source: The data suggest that HA trimers independently undergo the first part of their low-pH-induced conformational change and pause as extended intermediates with their fusion peptides inserted into the target membrane.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data and simulation results.

claim: Capture by the target membrane restrains a trimer from collapsing to induce hemifusion until 2–3 neighbors help generate sufficient pull to deform the membrane.
source: Capture by the target membrane restrains a trimer from collapsing to induce hemifusion until 2–3 neighbors help generate sufficient pull to deform the membrane.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations and simulation results.

claim: When the conditions for hemifusion have been met, the final HA rearrangements are fast and cooperative.
source: This interpretation also argues that when these conditions have been met, the final HA rearrangements are fast and cooperative.
evidence: This is an inference from the kinetic data and simulation results.

claim: There is no evidence for defined, lateral contacts between HA trimers.
source: There is no evidence for defined, lateral contacts between HA trimers
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of structural evidence.

claim: Any lateral contacts between HA trimers could not persist during the substantial changes in HA conformation and orientation that accompany the progression to hemifusion.
source: any such contacts, were they present, could not persist during the substantial changes in HA conformation and orientation that accompany the progression to hemifusion.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural knowledge of HA conformational changes.

claim: The accumulation of N extended HA2 neighbors will lead to an abrupt and cooperative event when the critical Nth molecule joins the cluster.
source: The accumulation of N extended HA2 neighbors, each fluctuating toward a more stable, fully collapsed conformation while pulling against the elastic restoring force of the two membranes, will lead to an abrupt and cooperative event, when the critical Nth molecule joins the cluster (rather like the abrupt consequence of adding a new member to the team on one side of a previously balanced tug-of-war).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the experimental data and physical reasoning.

claim: Evidence for the rapidity of the final HA rearrangements comes from the results of the simulation and gamma distribution analysis and the sensitivity of the derived rate constant to the mutations introduced.
source: Evidence for the rapidity of the final HA rearrangements comes from the results of our simulation and gamma distribution analysis and the sensitivity of the derived rate constant to the mutations we have introduced.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation and mutational analysis.

claim: Any additional steps not directly sensitive to the mutations must be faster than any one of the steps of fusion-peptide engagement with the target membrane.
source: Any additional steps, not directly sensitive to those mutations, must be faster than any one of the steps of fusion-peptide engagement with the target membrane.
evidence: This is an inference from the mutational analysis showing which steps are rate-limiting.

claim: Engagement of the fusion peptide with a target membrane requires formation of an extended intermediate to project it beyond the outer margin of adjacent HA1 heads.
source: Engagement of the fusion peptide with a target membrane requires formation of an extended intermediate to project it beyond the outer margin of adjacent HA1 heads (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural considerations.

claim: For an extended intermediate to form, the HA1 heads must dissociate from their contact with an HA2 loop (HA2 residues 58–74), and that loop must reverse direction and become itself a helix.
source: For an intermediate to form that resembles the inner core of the ultimate, low-pH triggered structure (as drawn for the extended structure in Figure 1A), the HA1 heads must dissociate from their contact with an HA2 loop (HA2 residues 58–74: see Figure 3D) between the short first α-helix (HA2, residues 38–57) and the long central α-helix (HA2, residues 75–127) (Godley et al., 1992), and that loop must in turn reverse direction and become itself a helix.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural knowledge and cited work.

claim: Extension of the central trimeric coiled-coil probably drives the loop-to-helix conversion, as the amino-acid sequence of the loop strongly favors such a conformation.
source: Extension of the central trimeric coiled-coil probably drives the latter process, as the amino-acid sequence of the loop strongly favors such a conformation (Carr and Kim, 1993).
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence analysis and cited work.

claim: The extended intermediate would project the fusion peptide no more than about 25 Å beyond the palisade of un-triggered HAs.
source: The structure thus pictured would project the fusion peptide no more than about 25 Å beyond the palisade of un-triggered HAs (Figures 1A and 6)
evidence: This is a calculation based on structural considerations.

claim: The intermediate that mediates arrest and hemifusion must be almost completely extended, at least for part of its lifetime.
source: In short, the intermediate that mediates arrest and hemifusion must indeed be almost completely extended, at least for part of its lifetime.
evidence: This is a conclusion from structural and kinetic considerations.

claim: Breaking the interactions that restrain the fusion peptide is rate-limiting both for virion arrest and for hemifusion at the pH of endosomes (approximately 5 to 5.5).
source: Our results show that breaking the interactions that restrain the fusion peptide is rate-limiting both for virion arrest and for hemifusion at the pH of endosomes from which influenza virus penetrates (approximately 5 to 5.5)
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mutational analysis.

claim: This interpretation is consistent with the dominance hierarchy of mutations that influence the threshold pH for fusion.
source: this interpretation is consistent with the dominance hierarchy of mutations that influence the threshold pH for fusion (Steinhauer et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous mutational studies.

claim: Mutations that affect the pH dependence of fusion map to a number of sites distributed across the HA2 trimer interface.
source: Mutations that affect the pH dependence of fusion map to a number of sites distributed across the HA2 trimer interface (Daniels et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous mutational mapping studies.

claim: Changes in the stability of the HA2 trimer interface will influence fluctuations from the equilibrium structure and hence the 'window of opportunity' for the fusion peptide to withdraw productively from its pocket.
source: Changes in the stability of this interface will influence fluctuations from the equilibrium structure and hence the 'window of opportunity' for the fusion peptide to withdraw productively from its pocket.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural dynamics considerations.

claim: The fusion-peptide contacts are conserved in all field-isolated influenza HA virions and form upon cleavage of HA0.
source: The fusion-peptide contacts, conserved in all field-isolated influenza HA virions, form upon cleavage of HA0 (Chen et al., 1998; Russell et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The stability of fusion-peptide contacts is critical for viral transmission during passage from one host or cell to another and during entry.
source: Their stability is critical for viral transmission, not only in the passage from one host or cell to another, but also during entry
evidence: This is an inference about the biological importance of the structural feature.

claim: Fusion will be relatively unproductive if it occurs before the pH has dropped enough to allow M2-mediated acidification of the particle interior, which induces dissociation of the eight ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) from the matrix protein M1.
source: as fusion will be relatively unproductive if it occurs before the pH of the surrounding compartment has dropped enough to allow M2-mediated acidification of the particle interior (Ivanovic et al., 2012), which induces dissociation of the eight ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) of the viral genome from the matrix protein, M1 (Martin and Helenius, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on viral entry mechanisms.

claim: Evidence for extended intermediates for other viral fusion proteins is largely indirect.
source: Evidence for extended intermediates for other viral fusion proteins is largely indirect.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: For HIV gp41, binding of peptides such as C34 and T-20 indicates that the inner-core coiled-coil must be present before the outer layer folds back against it.
source: The most extensive data are for HIV gp41, in which binding of peptides such as C34 (Chan et al., 1998) and T-20 (Wild et al., 1994), mimics for the outer layer of the final, hairpin structure, indicates that the inner-core coiled-coil must be present before the outer layer folds back against it.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on HIV fusion inhibitors.

claim: Outer-layer peptides from paramyxovirus F proteins similarly inhibit fusion.
source: Outer-layer peptides from paramyxovirus F proteins similarly inhibit fusion (Lambert et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to studies on paramyxovirus fusion.

claim: Electron microscopy of human parainfluenza virus 5 (PIV5) fusing with target vesicles shows a distance between viral and target membranes that corresponds to the gap expected for the putative extended intermediate of F.
source: Electron microscopy of human parainfluenza virus 5 (PIV5) fusing with target vesicles shows a distance between viral and target membranes that corresponds to the gap expected for the putative extended intermediate of F, which (unlike the HA intermediate) should project much farther from the viral membrane than does the pre-fusion form (Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to electron microscopy studies.

claim: The lifetime of an isolated extended HA intermediate can be as long as a minute or more, depending on pH.
source: the mean lifetime of the 'pioneer' extended HA in any patch can be as long as a minute or more, depending on pH.
evidence: This is derived from the kinetic data showing the time difference between arrest and hemifusion.

claim: A relatively long-lived extended intermediate could prove to be a clinically useful target for an influenza-virus entry inhibitor.
source: Thus, a relatively long-lived extended intermediate could prove to be a clinically useful target for an influenza-virus entry inhibitor
evidence: This is a speculation about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: The inherent lower limit to the stability of the pre-fusion HA combined with the requirement for coordinated action of multiple, independently-triggered HAs curbs the ability of a virus to escape inhibitor treatment by mutations that accelerate fusion-inducing rearrangements.
source: the inherent lower limit to the stability of the pre-fusion HA combined with the requirement for the coordinated action of multiple, independently-triggered HAs to induce fusion, curbs the ability of a virus to escape such treatment by mutations that accelerate fusion-inducing rearrangements.
evidence: This is an inference about evolutionary constraints based on the mechanistic findings.

claim: The only clinically approved inhibitor of virus fusion targets the extended intermediate of the HIV fusion protein, gp41.
source: The only clinically approved inhibitor of virus fusion targets the extended intermediate of the HIV fusion protein, gp41 (Wild et al., 1994; Kilby and Enron, 2003)
evidence: This is a statement of clinical fact supported by citations.

claim: Analogous inhibitors have been designed for paramyxoviruses, influenza virus and flaviviruses.
source: analogous inhibitors have been designed for paramyxoviruses (Lambert et al., 1996), influenza virus (Lee et al., 2011) and flaviviruses (Schmidt et al., 2010a, 2010b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to inhibitor design studies.

claim: The low surface density of the HIV-envelope protein and the indication that one HIV-envelope trimer may be sufficient to mediate fusion have led to the inference that a single, trimeric gp41 mediates fusion through a very slow fold-back transition.
source: the low surface density of the HIV-envelope protein (Chertova et al., 2002; Zhu et al., 2003), and the indication, from experiments with virions bearing mixtures of active and inactive spikes, that one HIV-envelope trimer may be sufficient to mediate fusion (Yang et al., 2005), have led to the inference that a single, trimeric gp41 mediates fusion through a very slow fold-back transition.
evidence: This is an inference from previous studies on HIV fusion, supported by citations.

claim: The data presented for influenza HA show that there can be a long-lived species analogous to the extended form of gp41, even when the fold-back transition itself is fast.
source: The data presented here for influenza HA show that there can be a long-lived species, analogous to the extended form of gp41, even when the fold-back transition itself is fast.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data comparing influenza and HIV fusion mechanisms.

claim: The long delay between HIV binding and membrane fusion may reflect a sequence of events similar to those in the model for influenza virus fusion, requiring recruitment of at least a second envelope trimer following attachment of the first.
source: We suggest that the long delay between HIV binding and membrane fusion may reflect a sequence of events similar to those in our model for influenza virus fusion. In other words, we propose that HIV fusion may require recruitment of (at least) a second envelope trimer, following attachment of the first.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal extending the influenza findings to HIV.

claim: The delay time in HIV fusion would be a combination of the time needed to recruit one or more additional envelope proteins and the time needed to activate them with CD4 and a coreceptor.
source: The delay time would then be a combination of the time needed to recruit one or more additional envelope proteins and the time needed to activate them with CD4 and a coreceptor.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic proposal for HIV fusion.
